items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon, Ask Questions, and Make Your Claim (CER): What causes the Southern Lights, the curtains of green and red light that people in Tasmania and Antarctica see in the night sky?

body.html: An open-ended prompt. We need a claim about what produces the Southern Lights (aurora australis), with reasoning.

Charged particles streaming from the Sun feel a magnetic force 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵 from Earth's field. The force is perpendicular to the velocity, so the particles curve and spiral along the field lines. The field lines of Earth dip into the atmosphere near both poles. Collisions there with oxygen and nitrogen atoms excite the atoms, and the atoms give the energy back as light.

answer.html: The Southern Lights are produced when charged particles from the Sun are guided by Earth's magnetic field toward the south polar region and collide with atoms high in the atmosphere, which then emit light. Sample questions for the board: "Why do the lights appear at both poles at the same time?", "Why do they get brighter after solar storms?", "Why is the main color green?" Your own CER chart must be your own work; this is a model starting point.

check.html: The claim uses only ideas from this module: the magnetic force on moving charges (Lesson 3) and light as an electromagnetic wave (Lesson 4).

items.title: Focus Question: How can moving a coil of wire near a magnet produce an electric current in the coil?

answer.html: When a coil and a magnet move relative to each other, the wires of the coil cut across the magnetic field lines. The motion induces an EMF in the wire, and if the coil is part of a closed circuit, the EMF drives a current. If the coil and the magnet are both at rest, or move together, nothing is induced.

items.title: Identify Crosscutting Concepts (Investigate, Lesson 1): Make a table of crosscutting concepts and fill in examples that fit a wind turbine that charges a battery

body.html: This is a class activity. For each crosscutting concept, find an example in a wind turbine that drives a generator.

answer.html: Cause and effect: wind turns the blades, which turn the armature, and the wires cutting the field induce an EMF. Energy and matter: kinetic energy of the air becomes mechanical energy of the shaft and then electrical energy. Systems: blades, shaft, magnets, coil, and battery form one system. Patterns: the induced EMF repeats once per rotation. Scale: a larger turbine with longer wire in the field and faster motion gives a larger EMF.

check.html: Your table should contain examples taken from your own reading; these are representative.

items.title: Investigate Electromagnetism (HS-PS2-5, online): Plan a test showing that a changing magnetic field makes a current in a coil and that the current direction depends on the motion

body.html: A plan for an investigation with a coil of 200 turns, a galvanometer, and a bar magnet. The online lab data are not available here, so this is a method and an expected result.
Faraday's induction: a magnet moving in or out of a coil connected to a galvanometer induces a current. Reversing the motion reverses the current.

answer.html: Connect the coil to the galvanometer. (1) Hold the magnet motionless inside the coil: no deflection. (2) Push the north pole in: the needle deflects one way. (3) Pull it out: it deflects the other way. (4) Repeat the push faster: a larger deflection. (5) Push in the south pole: the deflection reverses compared with the north pole. Fewer turns would give a smaller deflection.

check.html: All five results agree with the idea that only a changing field induces a current.

items.title: Figure 4 (Determine): A straight section of wire in a loop moves downward through a magnetic field that points to the left. What is the direction of the current in that wire, and in the other side of the loop?

body.html: The field → 𝐵 points to the left. Side A of the loop is a wire that runs away from you (into the page) and is moving down at this instant. Side B, on the other side of the loop, moves up. Unknown: the current direction in each side.
The right-hand rule gives the force on positive charges, which is the current direction: it is along →𝑣× → 𝐵.
Let right be 𝑥, away from you be 𝑦, and up be 𝑧. Side A has →𝑣= −𝑧 and →

Then ( −𝑧) × ( −𝑥) = 𝑧× 𝑥= + 𝑦. Side A therefore carries current away from you. Side B moves the opposite way (up), so its current flows toward you. The loop's two sides make one continuous path of current.

answer.html: In side A (moving down) the current flows away from you; in side B (moving up) the current flows toward you.

check.html: The two sides move in opposite directions in the same field, so their currents are opposite along the wire and join into a single loop.

items.title: Figure 6 (Get It?): A rectangular coil in a wind-turbine generator is shown in three positions: its plane perpendicular to the field, its plane at 45° to the field, and its plane parallel to the field. In which position is the induced potential difference greatest?

body.html: 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃, where 𝜃 is the angle between the wire's velocity and the field. The EMF is largest when sin𝜃= 1.

The long sides of the coil move perpendicular to its plane. When the plane is parallel to the field, the sides move perpendicular to the field lines, so 𝜃= 90° and sin𝜃= 1. At 45° the sides cut the field less directly, so sin𝜃< 1. When the plane is perpendicular to the field, the sides move along the field lines, so sin𝜃= 0.

answer.html: The potential difference is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field lines.

check.html: In the perpendicular position the EMF is zero, so the maximum must be in the other extreme.

items.title: Figure 8 (Identify): A hand-crank flashlight generator has an armature loop that is turned at 3.0 revolutions per second in a uniform field. In what position is the loop when the current is zero, and how many times each second does that happen?

body.html: Rotation rate = 3.0 rev/s. Unknown: the loop position for zero current and the number of zeros per second.
The current is zero when the long sides move parallel to the field lines and cut none. That occurs twice in each rotation.
The sides move parallel to the field when the loop's plane is perpendicular to the field lines. In each revolution that happens twice (once for each face of the loop).

body.alt: zeros per second = 2 × 3.0 rev/s = 6.0 per second

answer.html: The current is zero when the loop's plane is perpendicular to the field lines. This happens 6.0 times per second.

check.html: One full cycle of the AC has two zero crossings, and a cycle is one revolution.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (electric guitar pickup)

body.html: An electric guitar pickup is a coil wound around a magnet. A vibrating steel string disturbs the magnetic field near the coil. Two cause-and-effect links work in series: (1) plucking makes the string vibrate with its own frequency, (2) the changing field through the coil induces an EMF.

answer.html: The EMF in the coil has the same frequency as the string's vibration, so the amplified signal reproduces the note. A harder pluck moves the string faster and gives a larger EMF. The evidence is that a motionless string produces no signal and a vibrating one does. Knowing the induction effect and the string's effect on the field lets you predict that the pickup output is an electrical copy of the string's motion.

check.html: This is the same principle as a microphone, with the string playing the part of the diaphragm.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1, Challenge): A horseshoe magnet has vertical field lines. A wire between its poles is pushed to the right, and the induced current in the wire flows away from you. Which pole of the magnet, top or bottom, is the north pole?

body.html: 𝐵 is vertical (up or down). The velocity is to the right and the current is away from you. Unknown: which pole is north.
The current direction (force on positive charges) is along →𝑣×
𝐵. Field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole.
Let right be 𝑥, away from you be 𝑦, and up be 𝑧. Then →𝑣= + 𝑥 and the current is +𝑦. Try → 𝐵 up: 𝑥× 𝑧= −𝑦, which is toward you, so that is wrong. Try
away from you, which matches. So → 𝐵 points down. Field lines run from north to south, so they leave the top pole and enter the bottom pole.

answer.html: The top pole is the north pole (and the bottom pole is the south pole), since the field must point downward.

check.html: Reversing either the magnet or the push would reverse the current, so exactly one assignment fits.

body.html: 𝑉<sub>max</sub> = 340 V, 𝑅= 2.5 × 10<sup>2</sup> 𝛺. Unknown: (a) 𝑉<sub>eff</sub>, (b) 𝐼<sub>eff</sub>. Work (a):

items.title: 9 (Check Your Progress): Explain how the generator in a wind turbine produces electricity, and name the energy conversions

answer.html: The wind turns the blades, which turn a shaft connected to an armature of wire loops in a magnetic field. As the loops rotate, their sides cut the field lines, so an EMF is induced ( 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃). When the generator is connected to a circuit, the EMF drives a current. The sides reverse their motion relative to the field every half turn, so the current alternates. Energy conversions: kinetic energy of the wind to mechanical energy of the shaft to electrical energy.

check.html: A motor reverses the process, converting electrical energy to mechanical energy.

items.title: 10 (Check Your Progress): Could you make a generator in which the magnet and the coil are both fixed to the same rotating shaft and turn together at the same rate?

answer.html: No. Induction depends on the relative motion between the field and the wire. If the magnet and coil turn together, the field through the coil never changes and the wires never cut field lines relative to the magnet, so no EMF is induced. To generate electricity, one must turn while the other stays still, or they must turn at different rates.

check.html: Compare with the opposite design, a spinning magnet inside a fixed coil, which works because the relative motion exists.

items.title: 11 (Check Your Progress): A hand-crank flashlight lights an LED. Where does the energy for the LED come from, and why is the crank harder to turn when the LED is lit?

answer.html: The energy comes from you: chemical energy in your muscles becomes the mechanical energy of the crank, which turns the armature, which produces the electrical energy in the LED. When the LED is connected, a current flows in the armature loops. That current feels a magnetic force that opposes the rotation (Lenz's law), so you must push harder. With no load, no current flows and the crank turns easily.

check.html: The generator cannot create energy; the extra effort of cranking is the energy supplied.

items.title: 12 (Check Your Progress): In a headset microphone the diaphragm is pulled outward quickly toward the speaker and then held still. Describe the induced EMF

answer.html: While the diaphragm moves outward, the attached coil moves through the magnetic field, so an EMF is induced and a brief current flows in one direction. When the diaphragm stops, no EMF is induced and the current is zero. If it then moves back inward, the EMF reverses. A faster movement gives a larger EMF.

check.html: A steady position gives no signal, which is why the microphone responds only to changes in sound.

items.title: 13 (Check Your Progress): A generator with one loop pair produces 30.0-Hz AC when its armature turns at 30.0 revolutions per second. What change is needed to produce 45.0 Hz, and what rotation rate is required?

body.html: One complete rotation gives one complete AC cycle, so the frequency in hertz equals the rotation rate in revolutions per second.
To increase the frequency, turn the armature faster: 𝑓= 45.0 Hz ⇒rotation rate = 45.0 rev/s = 45.0 × 60 rev/min = 2700 rev/min

answer.html: Turn the armature faster, at 45.0 rev/s (2700 rev/min).

check.html: The EMF amplitude also rises, because 𝑣 in 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃 is larger.

items.title: 14 (Check Your Progress): Why does a generator's output potential difference increase when the armature has more loops of wire? Name another way to increase it

answer.html: The induced EMF is 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃, which is directly proportional to the length 𝐿 of wire cutting the field. More loops put more wire in the field, so the EMFs add and the total is larger. Another way is to turn the armature faster (a larger 𝑣) or to use a stronger magnetic field (a larger 𝐵).

check.html: Each factor (𝐵, 𝐿, 𝑣) appears to the first power, so doubling any one doubles the EMF.

items.title: 15 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): A student says, "The average current in an AC circuit is zero, so an AC heater should dissipate zero average power." Explain the error. A heater has a resistance of 10 𝛺 and a maximum current of 2.0 A; find its average power

body.html: Power is 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅, which depends on 𝐼<sup>2</sup> and is never negative. The average AC power is 𝑃<sub>AC</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>1</sup>
𝑅.

answer.html: The student confused the average current with the average of 𝐼<sup>2</sup>. The current is positive half the time and negative half the time, so it averages to zero, but 𝐼<sup>2</sup> is always positive, so the heater warms up in both directions. The average power is 20 W.

check.html: 𝐼<sub>eff</sub> = 0.707(2.0) = 1.41 A and 𝐼<sub>eff</sub>

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon, Ask Questions, and Make Your Claim (CER): What causes the Northern Lights?

body.html: An open-ended prompt. We need a claim about what produces the aurora, with reasoning.

Charged particles (mostly electrons and protons) streaming from the Sun are deflected by Earth's magnetic field, because a magnetic field exerts a force 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵 perpendicular to the velocity. That force makes the particles spiral along field lines toward the polar regions. There they collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms high in the atmosphere. The atoms absorb energy, then release it as light.

answer.html: The Northern Lights are caused by charged particles from the Sun that are steered by Earth's magnetic field toward the poles and excite atmospheric atoms, which then emit light (green light mostly comes from oxygen). Sample questions for the board: "Why are the lights only seen near the poles?", "Why are they different colors?", "Why did the 1989 solar storm cause a power outage?" The evidence you collect (force on moving charges, circular paths in a magnetic field, electromagnetic waves) is revisited in the Module Wrap-Up. Your own CER chart must be your own work; this is a model starting point.

check.html: The claim uses only ideas from this module: magnetic force on moving charges (Lesson 3) and light as an electromagnetic wave (Lesson 4).

items.title: Focus Question: How can a magnet generate a current?

answer.html: When a magnet and a wire move relative to each other (or the magnetic field around the wire changes), the wire cuts magnetic field lines. That induces an EMF in the wire, and if the wire is part of a closed circuit the EMF drives a current. A stationary magnet beside a stationary wire induces nothing.

items.title: Identify Crosscutting Concepts (Investigate, Lesson 1)

body.html: This is a class activity: make a table of crosscutting concepts and fill in examples as you read.

answer.html: Cause and effect: moving a wire through a magnetic field causes an induced EMF. Energy and matter: mechanical energy turned into electrical energy in a generator. Systems: a generator is a system of magnets, a rotating armature, and an external circuit. Patterns: the induced current in a rotating loop repeats sinusoidally. Structure and function: the iron core of an armature concentrates magnetic flux.

check.html: Your table should contain examples taken from your own reading; these are representative.

items.title: Investigate Electromagnetism (HS-PS2-5, online)

body.html: A plan for an investigation showing (1) a current produces a magnetic field and (2) a changing magnetic field produces a current. The online lab data are not available here, so this is a method and an expected result.
Oersted: a current deflects a compass. Faraday: a magnet moving in or out of a coil connected to a galvanometer induces a current.

answer.html: (1) Place a compass near a wire carrying current from a battery; the needle deflects, and reverses when the current reverses. (2) Connect a coil to a sensitive ammeter and push a bar magnet in, hold it still, and pull it out. The meter deflects only while the magnet moves, in opposite directions for in and out, and the deflection is larger for faster motion or more coil turns.

check.html: Both results fit the book's statement that only a changing field induces current.

items.title: Figure 4 (Determine): What is the direction of the current when the loop is horizontal to the field, as shown?

body.html: In Figure 4 the field points from the N pole (left) to the S pole (right). The loop rotates about its long axis. One long side (near the S pole) moves up and the other (near the N pole) moves down. Unknown: current direction.
Use the right-hand rule from Figure 2: thumb along the wire's velocity, fingers along → 𝐵, palm gives the force on positive charges, and so the current direction.

The side moving up has velocity up and field to the right. Up crossed with right gives a direction along the wire pointing toward the closed end of the loop (the end sitting between the poles). The side moving down has velocity down, so its current points the opposite way, back out toward the open end. The current therefore flows in along the up-moving side, across the end, and out along the down-moving side.

answer.html: Along the side that is moving up (the S-pole side) the current flows toward the end of the loop that lies between the poles, then returns along the side that is moving down. This is the position of maximum current; half a turn later the directions are reversed.

check.html: The two long sides move in opposite directions in the same field, so their forces on charges point in opposite directions along the wire, which makes one continuous loop of current.

items.title: Figure 6 (Get It?): At what position is the wire loop when the potential difference is greatest?

body.html: 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃 is largest when 𝜃= 90°, that is, when the sides 𝑎𝑑 and 𝑏𝑐 move perpendicular to the field.
The sides move perpendicular to → 𝐵 when the loop's plane is horizontal and parallel to the field lines (the "horizontal" position in Figure 5, left). Then sin𝜃= 1.

answer.html: The potential difference is greatest when the loop is horizontal, with its plane parallel to the magnetic field lines, so the sides 𝑏𝑐 and 𝑎𝑑 cut straight across the field.

check.html: At the vertical position the sides move parallel to the field, sin0° = 0, and the EMF is zero, as the book says.

items.title: Figure 8 (Identify): In what position is the armature when current is zero?

answer.html: The current is zero when the armature loop is vertical, with its plane perpendicular to the field lines, so the long sides move parallel to the field and do not cut field lines (middle of Figure 5). This happens twice per rotation.

check.html: Consistent with the graph, where the current crosses zero twice per cycle.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (microphone, Figure 3)

body.html: Two cause-and-effect links work in series. (1) Sound waves cause the diaphragm to vibrate with the sound's pattern. (2) The diaphragm moves the attached coil through a magnetic field, and a wire moving through a field has an EMF induced in it (𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃).

answer.html: Since the coil's velocity follows the diaphragm's vibration, the induced EMF has the same frequency as the sound, and louder sound moves the coil faster so the EMF is larger. The evidence is the book's statement that microphone EMFs vary with the sound's frequency and are about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> V (then amplified). So knowing the induction effect on the wire and the effect of sound on the diaphragm lets you predict the microphone output: it is an electrical copy of the sound wave.

check.html: A microphone works like an earbud run in reverse, as the book states.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1, Challenge): Horseshoe magnet with vertical field lines; wire pulled toward you gives current right to left. Which pole is north?

body.html: → 𝐵 is vertical (up or down). The wire's velocity is toward you. The current (force on positive charges) is from right to left. Unknown: which pole (top or bottom) is north.
Use the right-hand rule: thumb along →𝑣, fingers along → 𝐵, palm gives the force on positive charges (the current direction). Field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole.

Let right be 𝑥, away from you be 𝑦, and up be 𝑧. The velocity is −𝑦 (toward you), and the current is −𝑥 (right to left). The force direction is →𝑣× → 𝐵. Try → 𝐵 up (+𝑧): ( −𝑦) × ( + 𝑧) = −𝑥, which is right to left, as required. Try
𝐵 down: that gives left to right, which is wrong. So
𝐵 points up. Field lines point away from north and toward south, so they point from the lower pole to the upper pole.

answer.html: The magnet's north pole is the lower (bottom) pole, and the south pole is on top, since the field must point upward.

check.html: Reversing either the magnet or the pulling direction would reverse the current, so exactly one pole assignment fits.

items.title: 9 (Check Your Progress): Explain how an electric generator works

answer.html: A generator has wire loops wound on an iron armature that is turned by an outside source of mechanical energy (wind, falling water, steam) inside a magnetic field. As the loops rotate, their sides cut field lines, so an EMF is induced in them (𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃). When the generator is connected to a circuit, the EMF drives a current. Because the sides reverse their direction relative to the field every half turn, the current reverses every 180° (AC with slip rings) or is kept in one direction with a commutator (DC). Mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy.

check.html: This is the reverse of a motor, which converts electrical to mechanical energy.

items.title: 10 (Check Your Progress): Could you make a generator with permanent magnets on a rotating shaft and a stationary coil?

answer.html: Yes. Induction depends only on the relative motion between the field and the wire. If the magnets rotate past a fixed coil, the magnetic field through the coil changes continuously, which induces an EMF (and, in a closed circuit, a current), just as when the coil rotates. Many real generators are built this way, and it avoids sliding electrical contacts.

check.html: Moving a magnet past a coil is Faraday's original type of experiment.

items.title: 11 (Check Your Progress): Bike generator: what is the energy source for the bulb on a flat road?

answer.html: The energy comes from you: chemical energy in your body is converted to the mechanical energy of pedaling, which turns the generator's armature, which produces the electric energy in the bulb. On flat ground you have to pedal harder when the light is on, because the induced current creates a magnetic force that opposes the armature's rotation (Lenz's law), consistent with conservation of energy.

check.html: Energy cannot be created by the generator; it must be supplied by the rider.

items.title: 12 (Check Your Progress): Microphone, Figure 3: what happens when the diaphragm is pushed in?

answer.html: Pushing the diaphragm in moves the attached coil through the magnetic field. The moving wire has an EMF induced in it, so a brief current appears in the coil in one direction. When the diaphragm moves back out, the coil moves the opposite way and the induced EMF and current reverse. The faster the diaphragm moves, the larger the EMF, and no EMF is induced while it is motionless.

check.html: Alternating motion gives an alternating signal, which is how the microphone copies the sound wave.

items.title: 13 (Check Your Progress): What changes to a generator are required to increase frequency?

answer.html: Turn the armature faster. One complete rotation gives one complete AC cycle, so the frequency (cycles per second) equals the rotation rate. (The 60-Hz U.S. grid means 60 rotations per second for a one-loop-pair generator.)

check.html: The EMF magnitude also rises with speed (𝑣 is larger), so the amplitude changes too.

items.title: 14 (Check Your Progress): Why does the output potential difference increase with a stronger field? What is another way to increase it?

answer.html: The induced EMF is 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃, which is directly proportional to 𝐵: a stronger field means each wire cuts more field per second, so a larger EMF. Another way is to increase the speed 𝑣 (turn the armature faster), or to increase the length 𝐿 of wire in the field by adding more loops (or larger loops).

check.html: Each factor (𝐵, 𝐿, 𝑣) appears to the first power in the equation, so doubling any one doubles the EMF.

items.title: 15 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): "Why does AC dissipate power? The energy going into a lamp when the current is positive is removed when the current is negative."

answer.html: The student's reasoning is wrong because the power dissipated depends on 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 (or 𝐼𝑉), not on 𝐼. Current squared is never negative, so the lamp heats and glows with either current direction. The electrical energy delivered is converted to thermal and light energy and is not recovered when the current reverses. The graph of power versus time in Figure 8 is always positive, with an average of 𝑃<sub>AC</sub> = 𝐼<sub>eff</sub> <sup>2</sup> 𝑅=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑃<sub>max</sub>, which is not zero.

check.html: The effective current is defined precisely so that 𝐼<sub>eff</sub> <sup>2</sup> 𝑅 equals the average AC power.
